newsitem.title: SPAIN: Argentina, Mexico say do not fear Fed tightening.
newsitem.headline: Argentina, Mexico say do not fear Fed tightening.

text.p: Mexico and Argentina said on Monday their markets were unlikely to be severely impacted by any change in the U.S. interest rate environment.
Financial markets are eyeing them closely amid fears the U.S. Federal Reserve may raise interest rates at its next policy meeting on March 25.

Of the Latin American nations, Mexico and Argentina are usually considered the most vulnerable to U.S. monetary policy -- Argentina because its currency is pegged to the dollar, and Mexico because the bulk of exports go to the United States.

"This time we believe that the risk is not very high -- why? because the tightening we're talking about of 50 to 75 basis points over the year is in whole or in part reflected in the long rate already," said Argentina's Undersecretary of Finance Miguel Kiguel.

"In terms of the cost to Latin America, and the cost of funds to Argentina, an increase in interest rates will not imply an increase in cost because there has (already) been a significant reduction in the spread," said Kiguel at a presentation on the edges of the 38th annual meeting of the Inter-American Development Bank. he added.

"The most likely scenario is 50 to 75 basis points -- we think that is very manageable and won't lead to a significant impact on the region," he said. "The story would be different if we were talking about a few hundred basis points."
A series of U.S. interest rate rises that started this time three years ago wrought havoc across the world's bond markets.
While investors may be worried about the impact on Latin American markets, most do not believe 1997 will see a repetition of the 1994 scenario.
Mexico's deputy finance minister Martin Werner told the same meeting his country was much less exposed to the negative impact of a possible U.S. rate rise.
"Mexico is much less vulnerable today than in the past," he said, citing a forecast current account deficit of $5 or $6 billion for 1996-97 compared with $30 billion in 1993-94.

He said Mexico should also receive some protection from levels of foreign direct investment, expected to total some $7 to $8 billion this year, while the size of its foreign reserves -- almost $20 billion -- would also help strengthen its position.
"We need a higher level but it is safer than in the past two years," he said.
Mexico could also take comfort from the fact it has little more debt to refinance this year.
Less than one third of its external debt was tied up in floating rate instruments, while the country had already included the prospect of U.S. tightening in its 1997 budget.
"We will never say it has no effect, but the effect will be related to whether the U.S. tightens more than expected," he added. --Barcelona newsroom + 34 3 424 2659
